items.title: The economics of investment expensing
items.summary:
In July 2025, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act made 100% equipment expensing permanent after two decades of temporary bonus depreciation. I evaluate this reform in a general-equilibrium heterogeneous-firm model with collateral constraints and nonrefundable tax deductions. When matched to U.S. tax-return and Compustat moments, the model yields three findings. First, permanent expensing raises long-run capital by 4.5% and output and real wages by 1.1%, roughly double the gains without financial frictions. Per present-value dollar of forgone corporate tax revenue, expensing builds 5.6 times as much capital as a tax rate cut, versus 3.4 times without financial frictions. Second, first-year capital purchases are U-shaped in firm age: young constrained firms and mature profitable firms expand, whereas unconstrained middle-aged firms whose investment exceeds taxable income delay purchases. Third, making expensing permanent gives up countercyclical bonus depreciation; enacted at the onset of a recession, a two-year bonus offsets 44% of the five-year investment drop.

Here is the paper by Doruk Gökalp , who is on the job market this year from NYU.

The post The economics of investment expensing appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .

items.title: Was Achilles Conscious?
items.summary:
Homer’s Greeks had no inner life . That’s the title of a recent introduction to Julian Jaynes’s bicameral theory of mind. To recap: in The Origin of Consciousness in the Breakdown of the Bicameral Mind , Jaynes argued that intelligent behavior preceded introspective consciousness. People could speak, learn, farm, build cities, and solve problems without mentally representing themselves as an “I” deliberating within an internal world.

In Jaynes’s theory, routine behavior followed habit but difficult or unfamiliar situations triggered “command hallucinations,” voices experienced as gods, ancestors, or rulers giving instructions. One part of the mind issued commands; another obeyed—hence “bicameral.” Increasing complexity, migration, and the breakdown of established authority undermined the bicameral mind. Starting around 1200 BC, roughly between the Iliad and the Odyssey, people increasingly began imagining alternatives and narrating their own actions within an internal mental space, in short, they became conscious. Consciousness was thus not a biological given but a product of cultural and linguistic evolution.

I used to dismiss Jaynes’s theory completely, The idea of otherwise normal but unconscious human beings seemed absurd. Today, I am not so sure. If you think AIs are not conscious, then a central premise of Jaynes’s theory becomes much more plausible: namely, a civilization of thinking, talking doing, but unconscious beings. The AIs are an existence proof. That said, I still find the evidence for a sharp break around the Homeric era weak. Linguistic differences…
items.t: Was Achilles Conscious?

items.title: Me on the cyberattacks
items.summary:
Tyler Cowen: Don’t Be Fooled By Randomness 
 The problems are serious, but the sky is not falling in. When it comes to the recent service outages, keep a few points in mind.

First, cyber risk is considerably higher than it used to be. Due to progress in AI systems, cyber offense has outraced cyber defense. Plenty of experts are attesting that a wide variety of systems can be hacked using advanced AI agents.

Second, not every reported incident is a cyberattack. In many cases we do not know, or somebody knows (one way or the other) and is not telling us. One possibility is that these are normal service outages but the world is paying more attention, so the number of problems appears to be spiraling out of control. Another is that institutions are patching or upgrading their systems to limit future cyberattacks, and something in the upgrade goes wrong, causing an outage.

For instance, Microsoft’s November 12 outage , the FAA’s November 13 ground stop , and JPMorgan Chase’s November 16 outage all seem to have been something other than direct cyberattacks.

Do not be too ready to look for patterns in the data, and recall the title of Nassim Taleb’s book: Fooled by Randomness .

Third, the risk of a larger and costlier AI-driven cyberattack remains real. The United States has redundancy and protective systems built into its national security establishment, its financial institutions, and its basic infrastructure. But those protections are imperfect, and with enough attempts somebody might break through and cause real damage.

We do need an emergency national emphasis on cyber…
items.t: Me on the cyberattacks

items.title: What should I ask Alexander Mikaberidze?
items.summary:
He is the author and the new and excellent The Louisiana Purchase: The Grand Bargain and the Making of America .  He also wrote The Napoleonic Wars: A Global History , one of my favorite history books.  He has extensive other writings on the history of the Russian military during that same period.

From Wikipedia :

Alexander Mikaberidze ( Georgian : ალექსანდრე მიქაბერიძე ; born 27 January 1978) is a Georgian lawyer, author and historian who specializes in Napoleonic studies . He is a full professor of history and social sciences at Louisiana State University in Shreveport , where he holds the Ruth Herring Noel Endowed Chair for the Curatorship of the James Smith Noel Collection, one of the largest private collections of antiquarian books, prints, and maps in the United States. In 2025, he was granted the Boyd Professorship, the highest and most prestigious academic rank awarded by Louisiana State University.

He is a scholar and historian in the very best old-fashioned sense of the term, one of the most underrated writers and scholars today.  So what should I ask him?

items.title: The economics of Jensen Huang
items.summary:
Most of my assessment is very positive , but I will excerpt this bit from my latest Free Press piece :

Finally, the company was not built to withstand Huang’s departure. Too much authority and knowledge were concentrated in his hands, as evidenced by his practice of having about 60 different people reporting directly to him. Whatever you may think of that system as a day-to-day routine, it can turn disastrous when the person at the top leaves. No one else has collected and interpreted the information those 60 subordinates have imparted to the CEO. We will see how his interim successor Colette Kress does, but there is a great danger that a lot of the contextual understanding of the company and business departed with Huang.

Again, all those direct reports may have worked wonderfully when things were going great, but as a more general practice it is not resilient. Another way to put the point is that the very best CEOs make themselves at least partially dispensable, rather than indispensable. So a large share price decline, following Huang’s resignation, is a sign of his failures as well as his successes. As one set of commentators wrote recently : “the company was never built for him not to be there.”

And one of the very best Ben Thompson columns (gated!) is on Huang and Nvidia.

The post The economics of Jensen Huang appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .

items.title: Coffeehouses and the Scientific Revolution
items.summary:
Abstract Historians have long credited coffeehouses, venues for conversation where strangers met across social ranks, with fostering scientific contacts and activity during the Scientific Revolution. We test this claim in seventeenth-century London. Relying on newly geocoded records and a staggered event study across parishes, we find that the opening of the first coffeehouse in a parish is followed by a persistent increase in applied scientists and scientific instrument shops. Effects are concentrated among applied scientists with weak family ties to Oxford and Cambridge. Social connections that link craft skill to theory increase, and new shops turn toward experimental instruments. Across European cities in the seventeenth century, we similarly find that the numbers of applied mathematics titles and scientific instrument makers rise after a city’s first coffeehouse, relative to cities of similar size and growth. In a quantitative urban model calibrated to our parish- and city-level estimates, coffeehouses account for 31 percent of London’s applied scientists in the half century after the first one opened in 1652. These findings show that social institutions can raise the production and use of knowledge by broadening access to intellectual exchange beyond formal academic networks

That is a recent paper by Monir Bounadi and Jens Oehlen, noting that Bounadi is on the job market this year .

The post Coffeehouses and the Scientific Revolution appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .
items.t: Coffeehouses and the Scientific Revolution
